posts.title: 🚨 Jio uses a trademark it doesn't own. But is that LEGAL?
posts.author: TM Insight India | Trademark Law & IP Updates | Startup Brand Protection
posts.snippet:
🚨 Jio uses a trademark it doesn't own. But is that LEGAL?

One of India's most recognisable brands has an interesting detail hidden in its IPO documents. 👀

According to Jio Platforms Limited's own Red Herring Prospectus (RHP), the flagship “Jio” trademark is owned by its promoter, Reliance Industries Limited (RIL), and licensed to Jio Platforms under a Trademark License Agreement.

⚖️ But is this legally permissible?

YES. Under Indian trademark law, a company can use a trademark owned by another entity through a valid licensing arrangement, subject to applicable legal requirements.

📖 Sections 48 and 49 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 deal with registered users and registration as a registered user.

But here's the interesting part: Jio Platforms also disclosed the potential risks associated with its continued use of the trademark, including the possibility of the licence being terminated under specified conditions.

The takeaway? A company doesn't necessarily have to own a trademark to use it legally—but the rights and terms governing that use matter.

📌 Read the company's own disclosure:
https://lnkd.in/g4uCSaUp

📌 The law: Sections 48 and 49, Trade Marks Act, 1999.

Follow @TMInsightIndia for more real-world trademark cases, legal insights and intellectual property breakdowns.

💬 Did you know this arrangement was legally possible?

#Jio #JioIPO #TrademarkLaw #IntellectualProperty #BrandProtection #TradeMarksAct1999 #TMInsightIndia
posts.reason: Real-world trademark licensing case study from India is solid IP content that could interest startups and GCs thinking about brand and licensing strategy.

comments.text: Worth flagging that this is standard group IP practice, not a Jio-specific workaround — the parent typically holds the brand across the portfolio and licenses it down so the mark survives restructurings or subsidiary sales untouched. The disclosure point about termination risk is exactly why investors should read the licence terms, not just the registration certificate.
Does the RHP disclose whether Jio Platforms is actually recorded as a registered user under Section 49, or is this a bare contractual licence with no entry on the register?

We see this constantly in deal due diligence — a target's core brand sits with a founder's holding company or a group parent, and the licence terms only get scrutinised once an IPO or financing forces disclosure.

posts.title: Tokenizing Luxury Real Estate — Episode 5/6: The wrapper decides everything
posts.author: Jasmine C.
posts.snippet:
Tokenizing Luxury Real Estate — Episode 5/6: The wrapper decides everything

A token is a record. The legal wrapper decides what that record is worth.

1⃣ A bond is a security wherever it lives. In the UAE, that points to the financial free zones (ADGM, DIFC) or the federal securities regulator — not the virtual-asset route built for fractional property tokens.

2⃣ Net, not gross. Withholding tax and the investor's own holding vehicle can move the real return a lot. Serious issuers show investors a net-return view for their country and structure before they decide.

In Tokyo yesterday, Fendi Casa, List Sotheby's International Realty - Tokyo and The One Atelier announced Japan's first Fendi Casa branded residence: a renovated private house in Hiroo, about 1,000 sqm over four levels, due summer 2027. Proud to have our team at THE ONE Atelier on it.

The numbers shared at the launch say a lot. Branded residence projects worldwide are expected to nearly double by 2032, yet Japan holds only about 3% of Asia's supply.

Episode 5 in practice in my humble opinion: 

1⃣ The brand creates the demand. The wrapper decides what an investor actually owns. In Japan, real estate tokens sit inside securities law, usually as trust beneficiary interests or TK interests under the FIEA. They are not treated as crypto.

2⃣ Same house, different net. A Hong Kong family office, a Singapore holding company and a Tokyo individual will not take home the same return from one Hiroo residence. Japanese tax on the asset, the investor's home country and the vehicle in between all change the result.

Design is what you see. Structure is what protects you.

Next: the four-stage architecture that ties it together.

When we published the first edition of our Global #Crypto Regulation Report in 2022, many markets had no regulatory framework for #digitalassets at all. Five editions on, most major markets have largely finished writing their rules.

The questions are now more practical. Can a transaction settle, be used as collateral, cross a border and hold up if someone in the chain fails?

When the answer is no, firms rely on exemptions, side agreements and manual workarounds. That's how a lot of innovation gets started, but it gets expensive. A cheap licence can come with bespoke legal opinions, parallel registers and a short list of counterparties willing to deal with you.

That's a big part of this year's edition, which covers more than 30 jurisdictions. Thanks to the more than 100 colleagues across the PwC network who wrote the local analysis.

posts.title: Your crypto provider has a MiCA licence.
posts.author: Dr. Ihor Hrabovych
posts.snippet:
Your crypto provider has a MiCA licence.
That does not make every stablecoin on its platform compliant.

For a business building payments around stablecoins, this distinction belongs in the product design.

On 8 October, ESMA set out its supervisory view: CASPs should not provide services involving stablecoins that fail the applicable MiCA requirements for asset-referenced or e-money tokens.

One detail deserves more attention: ESMA considers risk warnings and customer acknowledgements insufficient to compensate for missing issuer safeguards.

A customer ticking "I understand the risks" does not resolve that problem.

Consider a merchant using a stablecoin to collect revenue and pay suppliers. The provider's authorisation matters. So does whether that specific token can continue to be supported for the intended service.

If access has to be wound down, the merchant needs a workable alternative. Conversion, settlement timing and supplier acceptance become operating questions.

I would want three answers before committing:

• Which legal entity provides the service, and what does its authorisation cover?
• What supports the token's compliance assessment, including the issuer and redemption arrangements?
• How do payments continue if support for that token changes?

The opinion envisages narrowly limited, supervised wind-down arrangements to protect existing clients. That should not be mistaken for permission to keep the same product running indefinitely.

My concern is the shortcut: treating a provider's licence as due diligence on everything it offers.

When your team approves a stablecoin payment partner, who owns the token-level assessment?

#MiCA #Stablecoins #Payments
posts.reason: Substantive discussion of MiCA compliance for stablecoin payment products directly addresses CASP authorisation concerns and token-level assessment—core work for Lemur Legal's target buyers.

comments.text: This tracks with how ESMA has been treating CASP obligations more broadly — the authorisation covers the service provider's own conduct, not a blanket endorsement of every instrument it lists, and that distinction gets lost in a lot of commercial onboarding conversations.

Does ESMA's view extend to CASPs that only provide custody or transfer services for a stablecoin, or is the supervisory concern specifically aimed at those facilitating exchange and payment use cases?

We've had exactly this conversation with payment-focused clients — the instinct is to treat the provider's MiCA licence as the due diligence item, when the actual question is always one level down, at the token issuer's redemption and reserve arrangements.

Criterio de selección en coberturas sanitarias: los 5 factores determinantes. 💼🩺

Claves de auditoría previa antes de concertar una póliza:
• Capilaridad y proximidad asistencial: disponibilidad real de especialistas e infraestructuras hospitalarias en el radio operativo del asegurado.
• Alcance hospitalario y quirúrgico: blindaje ante contingencias de alta complejidad médica.
• Estructura de copagos: adecuación actuarial entre frecuencia estimada de uso y ahorro en prima fija.
• Trazabilidad de carencias: conocimiento preciso de los plazos de carencia y opciones de convalidación por antigüedad en el sector asegurador.
• Ecosistema digital: disponibilidad de telemedicina resolutiva y canales de gestión documental inmediata vía app.

FinTech is expanding across borders. But the real competition goes far beyond geography. 🌍

Digital banking, AI security, alternative payments, and crypto adoption are all moving in interesting directions.

Here are 7 FinTech developments worth paying attention to 👇

1️⃣ ZEN.COM × Mastercard — Pay by Bank Expansion 🇪🇺
The companies are expanding Pay by Bank across nine European markets, giving consumers more ways to pay directly from their bank accounts.
💡 My takeaway: Payment flexibility matters when it reflects real customer preferences.

2️⃣ Incognia — Rethinking Security in the AI Era 🤖
As AI agents become more involved in financial activities, Incognia is highlighting emerging fraud risks associated with automated financial decisions.
💡 My takeaway: Smarter financial technology needs equally strong security.

3️⃣ Monzo — Entering Spain's Digital Banking Market 🇪🇸
Monzo's expansion into Spain puts it alongside established players like Revolut, N26, bunq, and BBVA.
💡 My takeaway: Entering a market is one challenge. Earning customer trust is another.

4️⃣ Collect & Exchange  — Connecting Crypto Payments With Business Needs 🌐
As a CySEC-authorised Crypto-Asset Service Provider under MiCA, Collect & Exchange  (collectnexchange.cy) supports businesses exploring crypto payment acceptance and crypto-to-fiat conversion.
For international merchants, this offers a potential way to serve customers who prefer digital assets while supporting fiat settlement.
💡 My takeaway: Crypto adoption becomes meaningful when it solves a real business problem.

5️⃣ Revolut — Expanding Its Financial Ecosystem 🇱🇺
Revolut's move to establish a venture capital fund in Luxembourg reflects ambitions beyond traditional digital banking.
💡 My takeaway: FinTech competition is increasingly about building connected financial ecosystems.

6️⃣ mBank S.A. — Record Q3 2026 Performance 🇵🇱
Poland's mBank reported record quarterly profit, highlighting how banking fundamentals remain important alongside digital innovation.
💡 My takeaway: Technology matters, but sustainable financial performance still counts.

7️⃣ Itaú Unibanco — Expanding Crypto Trading 🇧🇷
Brazil's Itaú has expanded its digital asset offering to 15 cryptocurrencies, reflecting growing institutional interest in crypto services.
💡 My takeaway: Digital assets are becoming part of broader financial service strategies.

Here's what connects these developments for me:
FinTech isn't moving in just one direction.
Some companies are improving payment accessibility. Others are strengthening security, expanding internationally, or exploring digital assets.

But the underlying challenge remains the same:
Building financial solutions that people and businesses actually need.

posts.title: The UK crypto regime is not coming. The window is already closing.
posts.author: Cletus Utiome
posts.snippet:
The UK crypto regime is not coming. The window is already closing.

The FCA opened its cryptoasset authorisation gateway on 30 September. Firms intending to keep operating in the UK should apply by 28 February 2027, ahead of the regime coming into force on 25 October 2027.

Four months to apply. And an MLR-registered firm has to secure new authorisation through the FSMA gateway to keep operating. Existing registration does not convert.

Which means a lot of firms are about to need financial crime people who genuinely understand digital assets. Not people who can spell blockchain. People who can look at a chain of transactions and say what is actually happening.

Here is what makes that harder than it sounds.

The principles have not changed. Know your customer still applies. Source of funds still applies. Monitoring, sanctions, suspicion, all of it still applies.

What changes is that the instincts you built over a decade were calibrated for a different environment. In a bank, opacity is the warning sign. On a public ledger everything is visible, and you still cannot see the thing that matters, which is who is behind the wallet. The transparency is real and almost beside the point.

Mixing services. Chain hopping. Wallet clustering. Exposure scoring. None of it is conceptually difficult. All of it is unfamiliar, and unfamiliar at twelve years in is its own kind of uncomfortable, because by then you are supposed to be the person who knows.

That is the part I think we avoid saying. The barrier is rarely capability. It is the reluctance to be a beginner again in front of people who think of you as the expert.

So to anyone in this profession watching that February date:

Your experience is not obsolete. It is what makes the new knowledge usable, because plenty of people understand the technology and far fewer understand what suspicion actually means.

But experience without learning quietly becomes a ceiling, and you do not notice it happening. You just find the interesting work keeps going to someone else.

The firms will get authorised either way. The question is whether we are the people they hire to run it.

#FinancialCrime #CryptoRegulation #DigitalAssets #AML

posts.title: 🌍 Can crypto really be sustainable?
posts.author: Professor Jian Wu
posts.snippet:
🌍 Can crypto really be sustainable?
On Monday, in my Sustainable and Responsible Investing course (MiM M2 Finance, NEOMA Business School), we put that question to Sami Gotrane — HEC Paris alumnus, PhD from Université Paris Dauphine- PSL, and a senior executive with extensive experience in French and Tunisian banking.

Crypto promised three things: decentralisation, greater efficiency, lower transaction costs. The reality is more nuanced:

• ⚖️ Decentralisation can create new dependencies — parts of the crypto ecosystem rely on major cloud providers such as AWS and Google Cloud.

• ⚡ Innovation can carry an environmental cost — Bitcoin's energy-intensive Proof of Work is a striking example.

• 💰 Low fees can surge during congestion, undermining the very promise of cheap payments.

And beyond fees, many cryptoassets lack reserves or contractual income streams — making valuations highly speculative.

Yet innovation is responding on three fronts:

• Ethereum cut its energy use by approximately 99.95% after moving to Proof of Stake.

• Layer 2 solutions can reduce congestion and costs. 

• Stablecoins like USDC seek to combine blockchain efficiency with price stability through reserves of cash and short-term US Treasuries — though financial and operational risks remain.

So perhaps the real question is no longer "crypto or traditional finance?" but how to combine blockchain innovation with the stability and safeguards of traditional finance to build a more sustainable financial ecosystem.

🙏 Many thanks to Sami for sharing his expertise and stimulating our students' critical thinking — and to our students for their curiosity and participation.

posts.author: OneTutor
posts.snippet:
Are students already outsourcing their thinking during studying?

We analyzed more than 600,000 chat messages between students and AI tutors deployed at 32 higher educational institutions to understand how students use AI-driven learning support provided by their professors.

Many studies show homework performance increases due to AI access and exam performance decreases, because the learning effectiveness is often compromised with plain LLM use by students. So we wanted to see, who does the thinking: student or AI tutor? What we found:

Matcha and Hojicha are often mentioned in the same breath, yet they differ fundamentally in how they are made and how they perform in a recipe.

Matcha starts with Tencha: shade-grown tea leaves that are steamed, dried and stripped of stems and veins before being stone-ground into a very fine powder. That process is what gives Matcha its vibrant green colour, smooth texture and umami-rich flavour profile.

Hojicha is created by roasting green tea at high temperatures, traditionally over charcoal. The leaves turn brown and develop warm notes of toasted grains, nuts and caramel. Ground into powder, Hojicha opens up a different flavour range for beverages and culinary applications, from lattes to baked goods.

For product developers, the choice comes down to the profile a product needs: the fresh, umami depth and colour of Matcha, or the warm, roasted character of Hojicha.

AIYA Europe’s whitepaper “A New Dimension of Japanese Tea” explains both in detail, alongside Roasted Matcha, which is made from premium Tencha rather than stems or mature leaves.

If you are a South African manufacturer/supplier still invoicing DRC mines directly, your customer now carries a compliance problem with your name on it.
In September, the DRC’s subcontracting regulator (ARSP) ordered two major Copperbelt producers to terminate contracts with 1,540 suppliers. At one operation, 955 of 1,427 suppliers on file were ruled ineligible. Two in three. Annual audits start in 2027.
The direct-supply route is closing. Procurement will not defend it.
The compliant route runs through an accredited Congolese subcontractor. That solves the law and breaks the credit. Your receivable moves from a mine with a multinational parent to a local SME that cannot fund 60-90-day terms on a grinding-media consignment.
I propose you sequence as follows:
First, contract an accredited subcontractor before the mine drops you.
Second, anchor payment to the mine’s approved invoice via a tripartite assignment of proceeds.
Third, wrap the residual exposure in short-term credit insurance.
Last, volume. Scaling a channel you cannot get paid through is a bigger write-off.
Trade Finance Africa, through its DRC joint venture is building that programme with mining houses, subcontractors, financiers and credit insurers, and structuring the subcontractor relationship that keeps South African vendors compliant and shipping into Haut-Katanga and Lualaba.
Comply, get paid, then scale. In that order.

posts.title: For anyone who hasn't been following it, Weil, Gotshal & Manges, one of the best-known law firms in the US, looks set to close. Its leadership told partners yesterday that the firm
posts.author: Matthew Searle
posts.snippet:
For anyone who hasn't been following it, Weil, Gotshal & Manges, one of the best-known law firms in the US, looks set to close. Its leadership told partners yesterday that the firm should be wound up. I've been following the story closely, so here's a quick summary of how it got here.

Weil had around 1,200 lawyers and revenues of about $2bn last year. It made its name in restructuring work, including the Enron case. In recent years, though, firms like Kirkland & Ellis and Latham & Watkins grew much faster on the back of the private equity boom, and Weil struggled to keep up.

Partners started leaving over the summer. The private equity co-head, the private funds co-head and another senior PE partner all moved on, mostly to Simpson Thacher and Paul Weiss. The London office lost its leading M&A partner to Sullivan & Cromwell, and its head of finance is going to Simpson Thacher.

In September, the corporate chair Michael Aiello left for Cravath and took five partners with him, including the co-head of M&A. By some estimates the firm has lost around 28 partners this year and hired 23.

In October things moved quickly. Merger talks with Willkie Farr & Gallagher fell through, and a few days later Ramona Nee, who was due to take over as head of the firm in January, said she no longer wanted the role. On Wednesday the management committee recommended an orderly wind-down, and partners are expected to vote on it in the coming days.

The part I find most striking is that this wasn't a firm in financial difficulty. Weil has very little debt and was still forecasting record results for this year. Once enough senior partners had gone, though, others began to question their own future there, and the departures fed on each other.

It's interesting to think about whether AI changes this. I've heard it argued that firms will increasingly use AI to capture everything they know about their clients, from past advice and deal history to preferences and the people involved. That knowledge would then sit with the firm rather than in a partner's head, which in theory makes a firm less exposed when someone leaves.

I can see the logic, but I'm not convinced it changes much at the top end. Clients still buy from people they trust, and when a partner moves, the relationship often goes with them, however good the firm's records are. AI might make the handover smoother for the clients who stay, but it won't stop a rainmaker taking their best clients with them.

For now, keeping your best people still matters just as much as the numbers.

The best career advice I heard recently wasn’t meant for cybersecurity. It fits it perfectly.
I was invited to speak to high school students about careers in cybersecurity. Just before my session, the keynote speaker gave a funny, personal talk with three pointers that apply at any age or career stage. Here’s how they map onto our field:
- Get in the room and be useful. In cybersecurity, the room is a capture-the-flag competition, a community meetup, or an internship. Early on, being useful counts for more than credentials.
- Your mind is a muscle. Exercise it, write, and protect it. Threats change every week, so the habit of learning is the job. Writing matters more than most expect: a finding that isn’t clearly reported may as well not exist.
- Build range and stay anchored. Security touches law, finance, psychology and engineering. Range is an asset. Anchor it in strong fundamentals and sound ethics.
I had prepared the practical material: what the work involves, which subjects matter, and where to study. But at 16, few of us can make an informed career choice. What sticks is a speaker who makes a field feel alive. That keynote gave me the spark, and I carried it into my session. The interactive questions from the students suggested that perhaps I was able to inspire. 
The lesson for those of us who mentor: to inspire, you need to be inspired first.

If an African Startup Exits and Nobody Sees the Price, Did It Happen?

Ibrahim Sagna | Executive Chairman, Silverbacks Holdings

Africa recorded 81 exits in 2025, its second-best year on record. 

Yet nearly 9 out of 10 venture exits on the continent never disclose a transaction price or multiple.

For a decade, the dominant narrative insisted Africa couldn't produce exits. The data proves otherwise. 

But when 88% of transactions happen in the dark, a deeper challenge emerges: a market without a public record cannot price itself. 

Instead, it gets priced from afar, with incomplete data and at a steep discount.

As Nana Appiah-Korang, CIO at Silverbacks Holdings, put it: "I don't think the continent is facing an exit problem. I think it's really a disclosure problem."

This opacity acts as an invisible tax across the ecosystem. 

Founders lose valuation benchmarks in follow-on rounds, secondary buyers struggle to price deal flow, and local pension funds, holding billions in assets, hesitate to deploy capital into an asset class whose track record lives in private emails.

Venture capital relies on a power law, but institutional investors cannot underwrite a power law they cannot see. 

Standardizing exit reporting, disclosing valuation bands, and contributing to shared databases transform isolated anecdotes into a track record that compounds.

Africa’s exits are already happening in plain sight. The continent will be priced fairly on the day it consistently publishes the receipts.

E-commerce platforms must not manipulate search results in a manner that misleads consumers or undermines the relevance of their searches.

When announcing a price reduction, platforms must display both the reduced price and the prior price.

4. Consumer grievance handling

E-commerce entities must provide complainants with a copy of the complaint as recorded by the grievance officer.

The amendments also strengthen the integration of e-commerce platforms with the National Consumer Helpline.

What does this mean for businesses?

Compliance cannot stop at having a grievance officer or a consumer-facing policy.

Businesses should review their advertising practices, pricing displays, marketplace arrangements, search-result processes and complaint-handling systems before the amended Rules come into force.

For brands operating online, the bigger question is:

Are your digital business practices designed to withstand regulatory scrutiny?

One thing I've learned from working with crypto projects over the years: the legal questions tend to arrive much later than they should.

I've seen projects with a great product, an enthusiastic community, a polished website and a launch date already announced. Everything seems ready. Until someone asks what the token actually represents from a legal perspective and whether it can be offered and marketed as planned. That's usually when things get interesting. And occasionally expensive.

I genuinely enjoy working with ambitious crypto projects, and I certainly don't think lawyers should be the ones driving innovation. But there's a big difference between involving legal advisors early enough to help shape a project and bringing them in two weeks before launch to fix problems that could have been avoided.

My advice? Build your token, grow your community, get people excited. Just don't leave the legal questions until the very end. It's much easier to adjust a plan than to undo a launch.

posts.title: One important UX lesson in crypto products: Visibility does not guarantee awareness.
posts.author: Olga Laskevych
posts.snippet:
One important UX lesson in crypto products: Visibility does not guarantee awareness.

I recently tested a swap flow where the selected networks were technically visible: POL → Polygon, and ETH → Ethereum. But I completely missed them. Why? Because my brain automatically processed the interface as: “POL” and “ETH” = full asset labels.

The network names were visually treated like secondary metadata with smaller text, lower hierarchy, and positioned underneath the token names.  And that creates a dangerous UX problem in Web3. Because the network is not secondary information.

In crypto transactions, the network directly affects compatibility, transfer behavior, fees, risk of mistakes, and asset destination. Yet many interfaces visually communicate chains as if they were optional details. This is the difference between information visibility and cognitive visibility.

A product can technically show critical information while simultaneously designing users not to notice it. And in crypto UX, that distinction matters a lot. Because users don’t interact with interfaces line by line. They scan, pattern-match, and rely heavily on visual hierarchy to decide what feels important.

Why Traditional Banks Are Embracing Tokenization ‼️

For years, #tokenization was largely associated with crypto-native companies and experimental blockchain projects. Today, some of the world’s largest financial institutions are exploring how the same technology could improve the way traditional assets are owned, traded and transferred.

The conversation has changed. Tokenization is increasingly being considered as a way to modernize financial infrastructure.

From experimentation to real-world transactions

Tokenization involves creating a #digital representation of an asset on a #blockchain or another shared ledger. Depending on the structure, that asset could be a security, a fund interest, a deposit or a commodity such as gold.

The appeal for financial institutions goes beyond issuing a digital token. Shared digital records and programmable processes could help connect activities that have traditionally been managed across different systems, including ownership records, transaction processing and settlement.

Progress is already visible in established financial markets. In July 2026, the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC) announced that it had processed real production trades using tokenized versions of securities held at its depository. The transactions formed part of its work towards a broader tokenization service. 

These initiatives show why tokenization is attracting attention: it could help institutions connect #assets, payments and operational processes in new ways.

Why infrastructure matters

Creating a digital representation of an asset is only one part of the equation. For tokenization to be useful in established markets, it also needs to work alongside custody arrangements, legal frameworks, reporting requirements and trusted service providers.

The International Monetary Fund has noted that tokenization could change how ownership and transfers are managed across financial markets. At the same time, it highlights the importance of managing risks associated with platforms, technology and faster-moving financial processes. 

Bringing the same thinking to gold

#Gold is one of the world’s most established assets, but the processes surrounding it can still be fragmented. Custody, ownership records, trading, settlement and financing may involve different providers and systems.

This is the challenge sGold is being built to address. The company is developing a connected operating network designed to link allocated physical gold held in custody with digital ownership records, transactions, settlement, reporting and financial infrastructure.

As traditional finance explores how tokenization can improve the way assets move and interact, sGold is applying that same infrastructure-focused approach to physical gold.

Institutional crypto infrastructure is largely built, yet 89% of family offices report no crypto exposure, according to JPMorgan's 2026 Global Family Office Report.

1. Anna argued that the stack unbundled because bundled models such as FTX failed in public, and that separately regulated providers stop one failure from spreading through the stack. Oliver agreed full separation is technically safer but said it trades away liquidity and product access, because crypto has no single clearing house.

2. Daily liquidity on staked assets has a cost at every layer. Anna explained that ETP issuers such as 21Shares and BlackRock hold an unstaked sleeve so redemptions never touch the unbonding queue. The 21Shares staked Ethereum ETF met about $48 million of first-half 2026 redemptions with no failed or delayed orders and was about 86% staked at the end of June. Oliver noted that at recent yields the loan cost against staked collateral can offset the staking reward entirely, which in his view makes liquid staking tokens the more practical trading collateral despite their own risks.

3. Oliver advised clients to ask a prime broker how it controls keys and what share of assets sits on third-party venues, instead of relying on balance sheet analysis alone. Anna put supported assets, compliance certifications and evidence records ahead of commercial terms and performance when choosing a staking provider.

4. With Coinbase custodying roughly 80% of US spot Bitcoin ETF assets, Antonio judged custody a larger concentration risk than staking and said every institution should have a business continuity plan for a provider failure, with sub-custody as the fastest fallback. Oliver expected custody to deconcentrate once custody beyond Bitcoin, Ether and Solana is counted, as banks build their own custody stacks for tokenisation.

5. Anna placed responsibility for the allocation gap on providers, describing a sales enablement gap in which clients want a banker or custodian they already trust to explain safety and accountability.

posts.title: AI Is Becoming a Narrative in Crypto. But Where Is the Real Value?
posts.author: MD DELOAR HOSSIN
posts.snippet:
AI Is Becoming a Narrative in Crypto. But Where Is the Real Value?

As a Web3 founder who has explored different areas of the ecosystem  from DeFi and DEXs to blockchain infrastructure and AI there’s a trend in the crypto market that genuinely concerns me.

AI has become one of the hottest narratives in Web3. And not every project using AI is building something meaningful.

Today, it feels like almost any project can add an AI feature, rebrand itself as an AI-powered platform, and attract attention from venture capitalists looking to invest in the next big trend.

Some projects combine AI with DeFi or DEXs. Others launch AI chatbots or products that resemble existing AI platforms. The problem isn’t combining AI with crypto. In fact, that combination has enormous potential.

The real problem is building around hype instead of delivering real value.

Over the past few months, I’ve noticed a growing number of projects that appear to prioritize fundraising, token generation events (TGE), and short-term gains over building sustainable products.

They generate hype, attract capital and users, launch tokens and then, in some cases, development slows down, commitments go unfulfilled, and the community is left holding the bag.

If this pattern continues, the consequences could be serious.

Retail investors may lose their hard-earned money. Trust in legitimate AI and Web3 innovation may decline. And founders who are genuinely building for the long term may find it harder to earn the community’s trust.

We need to remember one thing:

• AI integration doesn't automatically make a project innovative.

• VC funding doesn't guarantee product-market fit.

• A successful TGE doesn't mean a project has a sustainable future.

• Hype can attract attention, but only real utility, transparency, and execution can build lasting value.

Web3 doesn't need more projects chasing the AI narrative. It needs more builders solving real problems with AI.

As founders, investors, and community members, we should ask tougher questions before supporting the next hyped project.

What problem does it solve? Is the product genuinely useful? Does the team have a long-term vision? And will it continue building after the hype fades?

Because the future of Web3 shouldn't be about who captures the most capital during a trend.

It should be about who creates the most value long after the trend is gone.

What's your take? Are we witnessing genuine AI-driven innovation in crypto, or are we seeing another cycle of narrative-driven speculation?

posts.title: Italy has chosen legislation, not soft law, to bring AI into corporate governance. Listed companies must now describe their AI and IT-risk policies in the corporate governance repo
posts.author: Bruno Giuffrè
posts.snippet:
Italy has chosen legislation, not soft law, to bring AI into corporate governance. Listed companies must now describe their AI and IT-risk policies in the corporate governance report, where they have adopted any. 

What matters beyond Italy:

📌 The benchmark is EU law. Once AI systems are in use, the adequacy of a company's set-up is assessed against the AI Act, NIS 2, DORA and GDPR, which narrows directors' discretion. Fully autonomous systems are not seen as compatible with taking strategic decisions, which stay human.

📌 Evidence. A new law lets courts order disclosure of an AI system's logs, risk-management and technical documentation on a plausible claim, and treat the alleged facts as admitted if the order is ignored. It also reaches claims against directors and auditors, and certified compliance with the AI Act does not by itself rule out liability.

📌 Groups. The AI disclosure duty applies only to listed companies, but the duty to keep adequate organisational structures covers all businesses, so Italian subsidiaries are not out of reach. Corporate form still matters for the specific company law rules.

For insurers, one AI incident can lead to a claim against the company and, years later, to one against the directors based on the same grounds. Notification of circumstances, the line between D&O and cyber or tech E&O wordings, and underwriting questions on AI governance are worth reviewing now.

Directors should take and record every AI decision knowing that the documentation will be both their defence and evidence against them.

posts.author: Gus Neate

Seismic news in legal this week, Weil with >$2bn of revenue in talks on winding down. Few business models could have that much revenue and average profit per partner of $5.6M (with more for others) without debt and still be on the brink.

The thing is law firms are entirely based on the book of work from their top earners and are a confidence game. The chain of events that set this off is interesting.

Multiple star partners (often focussed on private equity - which is one of the most profitable practice areas) were poached to other firms like Cravath, STB and Paul Weiss. All great firms and their ability to lure over the partners is often either cultural or based on willingness to bet big with compensation that rainmakers plugged into their platform will perform.

Each poaching causes challenges internally culturally and concerns as partners and associates consider joining their often close colleagues. The best defence often here is offence with the firm "fighting back" and hiring a top performer from another similar top tier firm - which gets the narrative back to excitement and adds some juice into the team.

Weil looking at a merger with Willkie Farr looks more like a sign of real distress and law firm mergers have a history of integration challenges, given you can need to revamp compensation, internal structure and client books including things like conflicts. It's hard to keep those sorts of talks confidential when partnerships often would need buy-in from many people on both sides.

And crucially, the ultimate risk is that once you're in talks if it falls over, similar to in M&A generally, it can taint the target. People wonder "what did they find that meant they didn't move forwards?" - not always fairly, but the thought does cross the mind.

The nail in the coffin appears to be having Davis Polk confirmed at looking at options as at this point even the most loyal clients who are really the key to the firm's success are likely to evaluate their options and are likely to be hammered by other BigLaw for catch ups to capitalise on the changes.

Certainly feel for the people I know at Weil in these uncertain times. But given the extent of competition and business model challenges for law at the moment, I wouldn't be surprised if there are more similar stories in the coming years.

Luckily, top lawyers remain in very high demand and those at Weil are likely to see firms, in-house and AI companies all reaching out to provide a soft landing whatever the outcome. For the tech forward folk, do drop me a message - always happy to talk.

45% of EU tech founders paused or cancelled features because of regulation last year.
That’s from a 2026 survey of 155 founders by DutchBasecamp and CCIA Europe. It also found:

🔹 58% delayed entering another EU market
🔹 Nearly 1 in 4 spent over 30% of their budget on compliance

Much of that isn’t the cost of compliance. 

It’s the cost of finding out late.

CEPS put a number on the difference for the AI Act. Building a quality management system from scratch costs roughly €193,000 to €330,000, plus around €71,000 a year to maintain. Firms that already run sound processes pay far less, because half the work is already done.

The regulations I see founders miss most often:

European Accessibility Act. In force since June 2025 and still a surprise to most SaaS and e-commerce teams. Accessibility is architecture, not a CSS patch.

Cyber Resilience Act. Vulnerability reporting started in September. Security by design, SBOMs and years of security updates are very hard to add to a shipped product.

Data Act. Connected products placed on the market from September 2026 must let users access their data by design. That’s a data model decision, not a settings page.

Product Liability Directive. From December 2026, software is a product. Your documentation becomes your defence, even 5 years after you shipped a feature.

The hard part is that these don’t arrive one at a time. Ship one digital product in the EU and product safety, cybersecurity, data protection, sector and AI rules can all apply at once.

That’s what we are building. We work out every obligation that reaches your product across every EU regime, map shared evidence once so it satisfies them all, and keep your compliance state current as the product and the law change.

posts.title: Can I have your Consent? (Day3/30 of Simplifying data protection laws)
posts.author: Lisa Kukreja
posts.snippet:
Can I have your Consent? (Day3/30 of Simplifying data protection laws) 

"Don't worry, the data is anonymised."
Some of the most confident words in tech. Also some of the most frequently wrong.

Removing names and phone numbers doesn't make data anonymous. It makes it unlabelled.

Research by Latanya Sweeney famously showed that ZIP code, gender and date of birth alone were enough to uniquely identify most Americans. In India, swap in PIN code, college and employer and the effect is much the same.

What usually happens is pseudonymisation: names are replaced with IDs, but the dataset can still be linked back to a person.

And the law treats these very differently:
→ Under GDPR, pseudonymised data is still personal data. Recital 26 says that only data where a person is no longer identifiable, considering all means reasonably likely to be used, falls outside the law.
→ Under the DPDP Act, if data can identify a person, directly or indirectly, it's personal data.

Re-identification risk grows when you:
• Combine datasets ("it's anonymous on its own" is not a defence)
• Share data with vendors who hold other data
• Publish location, timestamps or rare attributes

Before calling a dataset anonymous, ask: "Could someone, with reasonable effort and other available data, figure out who this is?"

If the answer is "maybe," it isn't anonymous. It's just in disguise. 🥸

Have you seen "anonymised" data that turned out to be very much not anonymous?

Digital trade platforms don't talk to each other. Here's why that's a bigger problem than it sounds. 👇

A document that's legally valid in one country can be meaningless in the next. The same eBL can be encoded in ways that two platforms simply can't read. And even when the tech and the law align, competitors have little incentive to route their data through a rival's rails.

Three interconnected barriers keep digital trade fragmented:

🔧 Technical — proprietary data formats, APIs, and verification methods. Open standards exist (UN/CEFACT), but adoption is uneven.

⚖️ Legal — the legal status of electronic documents varies by jurisdiction. MLETR offers a framework for equivalence, but not every country has adopted it.

💼 Commercial — competing stakeholders create "walled gardens" rather than share infrastructure.

The result? A single-platform model hasn't cracked it — most solutions still require every party to onboard to the same system.

The emerging answer may be federation: independent platforms staying independent while still connecting. It rests on four pillars — standards, legal recognition, trust frameworks, and business incentives.
